newsitem.title: UK: Virgin, Sabena will compete with Eurostar.
newsitem.headline: Virgin, Sabena will compete with Eurostar.

text.p: British entrepreneur Richard Branson's Virgin Group confirmed on Friday that it will effectively be competing against itself with the start of new Virgin Express air services from London to Brussels from Sunday.

Branson's European short-haul airline is to take over the operation of Belgian carrier Sabena's nine daily services between Heathrow and Brussels, under a wet-lease deal whereby Virgin will operate the service for Sabena using Virgin aircraft in Virgin Express livery.
Virgin is already a shareholder in European passenger train operator Eurostar, with a 17 percent shareholder in Eurostar's British arm, London and Continental Railways (L&C).
Airlines have seen many passengers plumping for the train instead since Eurostar opened its London-Brussels and London-Paris services through the new Anglo-French Channel tunnel two years ago.
"We will be competing with Eurostar, and Virgin has a stake in Eurostar," Virgin Group director and chief spokesman Will Whitehorn said.
"But we do not see a conflict of interest since all of the Virgin staff who are involved in Eurostar are now employees of London and Continental," he said.

"Virgin is now largely a passive shareholder in Eurostar and this (airline) service will compete with them. But it will also open up more opportunities for cooperation such as fly/rail tickets," he said.
Eurostar and British Midland Airways already offer fly/rail tickets -- tickets which allow business class passengers the option of travelling one way by rail and the other by air.
Whitehorn also confirmed that Virgin felt the Sabena deal was also an opportunity that it could not afford to miss.
"We were approached by Sabena to operate this service for them and if they had not come to us to do it they would have gone to someone else," he told Reuters.
Eurostar said it would both compete and work with Virgin Express, just as it does with Virgin Express's Heathrow rival British Midland Airways.
Eurostar said it is now market leader with a 52 percent share of the London-Brussels rail and air market but it hopes to increase its share further.

"We are looking forward to working with them (Virgin Express) to look at the possibility of joint services such as interchangeable tickets," said Eurostar spokeswoman Debra Aspin, a former Virgin employee.

Eurostar's lowest return rail fare from London to Brussels is 59 stg return inclusive. Virgin said earlier it is offering an introductory air fare of 29 stg one-way before taxes, for purchases made by the end of October, and a standard fare of 32 stg one-way thereafter.
British Midland and British Airways both said on Friday that their lowest fare on the Heathrow-Brussels route was 85 stg return exclusive of taxes.
